episodes.content:
Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want to stay sharp, stay current, and stay clinical. I'm glad you're here today, because we're diving into something that sits right at the intersection of imaging technology and clinical decision-making. Something that, honestly, doesn't get talked about enough in day-to-day practice. We're talking about fundus autofluorescence, and specifically, how lipofuscin behaves as a disease marker in conditions like Stargardt disease, age-related macular degeneration, and hydroxychloroquine toxicity. If you've ever looked at a fundus autofluorescence image and felt a little uncertain about what you were seeing, this episode is for you.

Let's start with the foundation. Fundus autofluorescence, or FAF, is a non-invasive imaging modality that captures the natural fluorescence of the retinal pigment epithelium. The RPE is the star of this story. It accumulates a fluorophore called lipofuscin over time, and lipofuscin is essentially the metabolic waste product of photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis. When you shine the appropriate excitation wavelength at the fundus, lipofuscin emits a detectable signal. That signal is what we're reading when we interpret a fundus autofluorescence image.

Now here's why this matters clinically. Lipofuscin accumulation is not just a passive aging phenomenon. It is a dynamic marker of RPE stress, dysfunction, and cell death. When RPE cells are metabolically overwhelmed, lipofuscin builds up and you see hyperautofluorescence, a brighter signal on the image. When RPE cells have died or are severely atrophic, there's no lipofuscin left to fluoresce, and you see hypoautofluorescence, a darker signal. Reading these patterns correctly gives you a window into the health of the RPE-photoreceptor complex that you simply cannot get from a standard fundus photograph or even from OCT alone. FAF complements your OCT beautifully, and together they tell a much more complete story.

So let's talk about how to actually read these images in practice. Think of a normal FAF image as having a relatively uniform, mid-level gray background signal across the posterior pole. The optic nerve head appears dark because there's no RPE there to fluoresce. The fovea also appears slightly darker than the surrounding macula because of macular pigment, which absorbs the excitation light and reduces the autofluorescent signal. Blood vessels appear dark as well because the hemoglobin absorbs the excitation wavelength. Once you have that normal baseline in your mind, deviations from it become much easier to spot and interpret.

Hyperautofluorescence means more lipofuscin, more RPE stress, more metabolic burden. Hypoautofluorescence means RPE atrophy, cell death, or something blocking the signal from below, like subretinal fluid, blood, or pigment. Keep that framework in your head as we walk through each condition.

Let's start with Stargardt disease, because it is one of the most instructive conditions for learning FAF interpretation. Stargardt is the most common inherited macular dystrophy, caused by mutations in the ABCA4 gene. This gene encodes a transporter protein in photoreceptor outer segments, and when it's dysfunctional, a toxic bisretinoid called A2E accumulates in the RPE. A2E is a major component of lipofuscin, and in Stargardt patients, it accumulates at an accelerated and pathological rate.

On FAF imaging, Stargardt has a very characteristic appearance. You'll typically see a central area of hypoautofluorescence at the macula, representing RPE atrophy and photoreceptor loss. Surrounding that central dark zone, you'll often see a ring or halo of hyperautofluorescence, representing the zone of stressed but still viable RPE that is loaded with lipofuscin. And then scattered throughout the posterior pole, you'll see the classic flecks. These flecks appear hyperautofluorescent early in the disease, when they are composed of lipofuscin-laden RPE cells. As the disease progresses, those same flecks can become hypoautofluorescent as the RPE cells die. So in a single Stargardt patient, you may see both hyper and hypo signals, and understanding the temporal evolution of those signals helps you stage the disease.

One of the most clinically useful FAF findings in Stargardt is the dark choroid sign on fluorescein angiography, but on FAF specifically, the pericentral hyperautofluorescent flecks are your early warning system. If a young patient comes in with reduced best-corrected visual acuity that doesn't improve with refraction, a relatively normal-looking fundus on direct ophthalmoscopy, and subtle foveal changes on OCT, FAF may be the imaging modality that reveals the flecks and points you toward the diagnosis before the fundus looks overtly abnormal. That's the clinical power of FAF in Stargardt.

From a management standpoint, once you suspect Stargardt, your role as the optometrist includes genetic counseling referral, low vision evaluation, and co-management with a retinal specialist. You'll want to counsel patients on avoiding vitamin A supplementation, as there is evidence that excess vitamin A can accelerate lipofuscin accumulation in ABCA4-related disease. Sun protection with UV-blocking lenses is also recommended. And you'll want to monitor these patients longitudinally with serial FAF imaging to track the expansion of the atrophic zone over time.

Now let's move to age-related macular degeneration, where FAF has become an essential part of the imaging toolkit. In AMD, the RPE is under chronic oxidative stress, and lipofuscin accumulation is a central feature of the disease process. In early and intermediate AMD, FAF can reveal patterns of RPE dysfunction that precede visible changes on fundus photography.

In geographic atrophy, the advanced dry form of AMD, FAF is particularly powerful. The atrophic zones appear as sharply demarcated areas of hypoautofluorescence, because the RPE has been completely lost. But what makes FAF so valuable in GA is what you see at the border of the atrophy. The junctional zone, the area immediately surrounding the atrophic patch, often shows a rim of hyperautofluorescence. This hyperautofluorescent border represents RPE cells that are metabolically stressed and loaded with lipofuscin, and research has shown that the pattern of this border predicts the rate of GA progression. A diffuse or banded hyperautofluorescent border is associated with faster progression compared to a focal or none pattern. This is clinically actionable information. When you're counseling a patient with geographic atrophy about prognosis and monitoring frequency, the FAF pattern at the border of the lesion should inform that conversation.

In neovascular AMD, FAF can help you identify areas of RPE disruption and monitor treatment response alongside OCT. Subretinal fluid and pigment epithelial detachments can cause variable autofluorescent signals, and tracking changes in those signals over time adds another layer of information to your anti-VEGF co-management.

For your AMD patients, FAF should be part of your standard imaging protocol alongside OCT and fundus photography. When you see a new area of hypoautofluorescence developing in a patient you've been monitoring, that's a signal to expedite your retinal referral or to communicate urgently with the retinal specialist you're co-managing with.

Now let's talk about hydroxychloroquine toxicity, because this is an area where optometrists are truly on the front lines of detection, and FAF is one of your most sensitive tools. Hydroxychloroquine, sold under the brand name Plaquenil, is widely used in rheumatology for conditions like lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. It is generally well tolerated, but with long-term use, it can cause a characteristic bull's-eye maculopathy that leads to irreversible vision loss if not caught early.

The mechanism involves hydroxychloroquine binding to melanin in the RPE and causing direct RPE toxicity. Early toxicity is often asymptomatic and invisible on fundus examination. This is exactly where FAF earns its place in your screening protocol. Early hydroxychloroquine toxicity on FAF appears as a ring of hyperautofluorescence in the parafoveal region, corresponding to the zone of RPE stress before cell death occurs. As toxicity progresses, that ring transitions to hypoautofluorescence as the RPE cells die, creating the classic bull's-eye pattern of central foveal sparing surrounded by a ring of atrophy.

The American Academy of Ophthalmology guidelines recommend annual screening for patients on hydroxychloroquine after five years of use, or earlier in high-risk patients. Your screening protocol should include best-corrected visual acuity, Humphrey visual field testing with a 10-2 protocol, spectral-domain OCT, and fundus autofluorescence. On OCT, early toxicity appears as loss of the ellipsoid zone in the parafoveal region. On FAF, that parafoveal hyperautofluorescent ring may appear even before the OCT changes become obvious. Using both modalities together maximizes your sensitivity.

When you detect a suspicious FAF pattern in a hydroxychloroquine patient, your immediate action is to communicate with the prescribing rheumatologist. Do not wait. Document your findings thoroughly, send a detailed clinical note, and recommend discontinuation of the drug pending further evaluation. Refer to a retinal specialist for confirmation and co-management. The damage from hydroxychloroquine toxicity is irreversible, so early detection is everything.

Let's bring this all together. Fundus autofluorescence is not a specialty imaging tool reserved for retinal practices. It is a clinically essential modality that every optometrist managing posterior segment disease should be comfortable ordering and interpreting. The core principle is straightforward. Hyperautofluorescence means RPE stress and lipofuscin accumulation. Hypoautofluorescence means RPE atrophy or signal blockage. Apply that framework to Stargardt, AMD, and hydroxychloroquine toxicity, and you have a powerful diagnostic lens through which to view your patients' retinal health.

In Stargardt, look for the hyperautofluorescent flecks and the central atrophic zone. In AMD, track the junctional zone of geographic atrophy and use the border pattern to guide your prognostic conversations. In hydroxychloroquine toxicity, screen proactively and act decisively when you see that parafoveal hyperautofluorescent ring.

Your ability to read these patterns accurately protects your patients' vision and positions you as an indispensable partner in their care team. That's what clinical optometry looks like at its best.

Thank you so much for spending this time with me today. I hope this episode gives you more confidence the next time you pull up a fundus autofluorescence image in your practice. Keep asking the right questions, keep imaging thoughtfully, and keep putting your patients first. For more clinical content built specifically for eye care professionals, visit Focus Cast at Focuslinks dot in. Until next time, take care of your patients, and take care of your eyes.

episodes.content:
Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want to stay sharp, stay current, and stay clinical. I'm glad you're here today, because we're diving into one of the most powerful diagnostic tools in retinal imaging, and honestly, one that a lot of practitioners feel a little uncertain about when they first start interpreting results. We're talking about fluorescein angiography. Specifically, we're going to break down the phases, talk about what leakage really looks like versus a window defect, and give you a practical framework you can actually use when you're reviewing these images in a clinical setting. So whether you're a resident just getting comfortable with FA interpretation, or a seasoned OD who wants a solid refresher, this episode is for you. Let's get into it.

First, let's set the stage. Fluorescein angiography, or FA, has been a cornerstone of retinal diagnostics for decades. It involves the intravenous injection of sodium fluorescein dye, which then circulates through the retinal and choroidal vasculature. A specialized fundus camera captures the fluorescence as the dye passes through, and what you get is a dynamic, time-sequenced map of retinal blood flow and vascular integrity. Now, as optometrists, many of us are not personally performing the injection or operating the FA unit, but we absolutely need to be fluent in interpreting these images. Because when a retinal specialist sends back a report with an FA attached, or when you're co-managing a diabetic patient or someone with suspected choroidal neovascularization, you need to know what you're looking at. Your ability to interpret FA findings directly impacts your referral decisions, your urgency calls, and your patient conversations.

So let's start with the phases, because this is the foundation of everything else.

The fluorescein angiogram unfolds in a predictable sequence, and understanding that sequence is what allows you to interpret any abnormality you encounter. The first phase is the choroidal phase, sometimes called the pre-arterial phase. This occurs roughly eight to twelve seconds after injection, and what you see is a patchy, mottled flush of the choroid. The choroidal vasculature fills first because the posterior ciliary arteries supply it, and they receive blood before the central retinal artery fills. You'll often see the optic disc begin to show early fluorescence here as well. This phase is brief, and it's easy to miss if you're not watching carefully, but it's clinically important because choroidal filling defects can indicate conditions like giant cell arteritis or severe occlusive disease.

Then comes the arterial phase, which begins when the central retinal artery starts to fill, typically around ten to fifteen seconds post-injection. You'll see the retinal arterioles light up with bright fluorescence, moving from the disc outward. This is a clean, sharp filling pattern. The veins at this point are still dark. If you see delayed arterial filling, you should be thinking about carotid artery disease, central retinal artery occlusion, or severe optic nerve ischemia. Asymmetric filling between the two eyes is also a red flag worth noting.

Next is the arteriovenous phase, or the transit phase. This is where things get really interesting. The capillary bed fills, and you start to see laminar flow in the veins, meaning the dye flows along the walls of the veins first before filling the lumen completely. This creates a beautiful striped appearance in the larger venous channels. The entire retinal capillary network becomes visible during this phase, and this is where you'll start to identify microaneurysms, areas of capillary non-perfusion, and early neovascularization. In a diabetic patient, this phase is incredibly revealing. Microaneurysms appear as tiny, discrete hyperfluorescent dots. Areas of capillary dropout appear as dark, hypofluorescent patches with no capillary filling. And if there's neovascularization, you'll see a lacy, irregular network of new vessels that fill early and, importantly, leak profusely.

Then we move into the venous phase, which is subdivided into early, mid, and late venous stages. By the late venous phase, the veins are fully filled and the arteries are beginning to empty. The retinal background fluorescence is at its peak here. This is the phase where you're really scrutinizing for abnormal hyperfluorescence or hypofluorescence, and we'll come back to that in just a moment.

Finally, there's the late phase, also called the recirculation phase, which occurs roughly ten minutes after injection. By this point, the dye has largely cleared from the normal retinal vasculature. The background fluorescence fades. And here's the key clinical pearl: any hyperfluorescence that persists or increases in the late phase is almost certainly due to leakage. Normal structures don't retain dye. So if you see a bright spot that gets bigger and brighter as the study progresses, that's dye accumulating in tissue, and that means there's a breakdown in the blood-retinal barrier somewhere.

Now let's talk about the two most important concepts in FA interpretation: leakage and blocking. And let's add a third one that trips people up constantly, which is the window defect. Understanding the difference between these three patterns is what separates a confident FA reader from someone who's just guessing.

Leakage, as we just touched on, represents a breakdown in the blood-retinal barrier. The inner blood-retinal barrier is maintained by the tight junctions of the retinal vascular endothelium. The outer blood-retinal barrier is maintained by the retinal pigment epithelium, the RPE. When either of these barriers is compromised, fluorescein dye escapes into the surrounding tissue. On the angiogram, leakage appears as hyperfluorescence that increases in size and intensity over time. It's not just bright, it's expanding. Classic examples include choroidal neovascularization in age-related macular degeneration, where you'll see a subretinal neovascular membrane that leaks profusely in the late phase. Cystoid macular edema is another great example, where dye accumulates in the cystic spaces of the outer plexiform layer, creating that classic petaloid or flower-petal pattern in the late phase. Diabetic macular edema, disc edema in papilledema, and active uveitis are all conditions where leakage is a dominant FA finding.

Now, blocking is the opposite. Blocking refers to hypofluorescence caused by something physically blocking the fluorescence from reaching the camera. Think of it as a shadow. The most common causes of blocking are preretinal or subretinal blood, hard exudates in large quantities, pigment, or any opaque material overlying the retinal vasculature. In a patient with a dense subretinal hemorrhage from a ruptured choroidal neovascular membrane, you'll see a dark, hypofluorescent area that corresponds exactly to the hemorrhage. The vessels beneath it are still there, still perfused, but you can't see them because the blood is blocking the fluorescence. Importantly, blocking does not change over time. It stays dark throughout all phases of the study. That's a key distinguishing feature.

And then there's the window defect, which is probably the most commonly misunderstood finding in FA. A window defect occurs when there is a focal loss or atrophy of the RPE. Normally, the RPE contains melanin pigment that absorbs and blocks the background choroidal fluorescence. When the RPE is absent or atrophied, that choroidal fluorescence shines through more brightly than it should. So you see hyperfluorescence, but here's the critical distinction: a window defect does not increase in size over time. It may increase in intensity early in the study as the choroid fills, but it does not expand. The borders stay sharp and well-defined throughout the entire study. This is how you tell it apart from leakage. Leakage expands. Window defects don't. Common causes of window defects include geographic atrophy in AMD, old laser photocoagulation scars, chorioretinal atrophy from high myopia, and resolved pigment epithelial detachments.

So your mental checklist when you see a bright spot on FA should be: is this getting bigger over time? If yes, it's leakage. If no, is it staying the same size with sharp borders? Then it's likely a window defect. And if you're seeing a dark area, is it corresponding to a known opacity like blood or pigment? Then it's blocking.

Now let's bring this into the clinical decision-making space, because that's where it really matters for your practice.

When you're co-managing a patient with diabetic retinopathy and the FA comes back showing areas of capillary non-perfusion in the macula, that changes your management conversation significantly. Macular ischemia is not treatable with anti-VEGF in the same way that macular edema is, and the prognosis for visual recovery is more guarded. You need to be able to communicate that to your patient and to the retinal specialist you're working with.

When you have a patient with suspected wet AMD and the FA shows a classic subfoveal choroidal neovascular membrane with late-phase leakage, that's an urgent referral. Same-week, if not same-day. Anti-VEGF therapy is time-sensitive in these cases, and every day of delay can mean additional photoreceptor loss.

When you're evaluating a patient with unexplained visual loss and the FA shows a branch retinal vein occlusion with significant macular edema and leakage, you're coordinating with retinal for anti-VEGF or steroid implant consideration, and you're also initiating a systemic workup for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypercoagulable states.

And when you see a window defect corresponding to an area of geographic atrophy in a patient with dry AMD, you're counseling them on AREDS2 supplementation, monitoring with OCT and Amsler grid, and discussing the emerging treatments in the geographic atrophy space.

FA doesn't exist in isolation. You're always correlating it with your clinical exam, your OCT findings, your fundus photography, and your patient's symptoms. The angiogram is one piece of a larger diagnostic picture, but it's a piece that carries enormous weight.

To wrap up, fluorescein angiography is a dynamic, phase-dependent study that tells you a story about retinal vascular integrity and RPE health. Know your phases: choroidal, arterial, arteriovenous, venous, and late. Know your patterns: leakage expands, window defects don't, and blocking creates shadows. And always tie your FA interpretation back to your clinical findings and your management decisions.

The more comfortable you get with FA interpretation, the more confident you'll be in your co-management conversations, your referral urgency calls, and ultimately, your patient outcomes. That's what this is all about.

Thank you so much for spending this time with me today. If you found this episode useful, share it with a colleague, a resident, or anyone in your practice who's working on building their retinal imaging skills. Visit Focus Cast at Focuslinks dot in for more clinical episodes just like this one. Until next time, keep your skills sharp and your patients' vision sharper. Take care.

episodes.description:
When fluorescein angiography leaves you with more questions than answers, ICG angiography may be the diagnostic tool your patient needs — and this episode shows you exactly when to reach for it.

In this clinical deep-dive from Focus Cast by Focuslinks.in, we break down the essential role of indocyanine green angiography in detecting choroidal pathology that fluorescein simply cannot visualize. Designed exclusively for licensed optometrists, optometry residents, and clinical eye care practitioners, this episode delivers evidence-based, chairside-ready guidance on three high-stakes scenarios: occult choroidal neovascularization in neovascular AMD, polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, and choroidal tumors including hemangioma and melanoma.

You'll learn why ICG's near-infrared fluorescence and protein-binding properties give it a decisive advantage over fluorescein when imaging beneath the RPE, how to recognize the clinical and OCT findings that should trigger an ICG-specific referral, what the EVEREST II trial data means for your PCV patients receiving anti-VEGF therapy, and how to differentiate circumscribed choroidal hemangioma from amelanotic melanoma using ICG's characteristic vascular patterns.

Beyond the imaging science, this episode sharpens your referral communication skills — because writing "evaluate for possible PCV, please consider ICG angiography" instead of a generic wet AMD referral can meaningfully accelerate your patient's diagnosis and treatment.

If you manage posterior segment disease, co-manage retinal patients, or simply want to elevate your clinical decision-making in ocular imaging, this episode is essential listening.

episodes.content:
Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want to stay sharp, stay current, and stay ahead in clinical practice. I'm glad you're here today, because we're diving into something that doesn't get nearly enough airtime in optometric continuing education, and yet it has the potential to completely change how you manage some of the most challenging posterior segment cases you'll ever see in your chair.

Today we're talking about indocyanine green angiography, or ICG angiography, and specifically why it sees things that fluorescein simply cannot. We're going to walk through the clinical scenarios where ICG becomes not just helpful, but essential. We're talking occult choroidal neovascularization, polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, and choroidal tumors. By the end of this episode, you'll have a clear framework for when to reach for ICG, what you're looking for, and how to make smart referral decisions that genuinely protect your patients' vision.

Let's start with a question. Have you ever had a patient with progressive vision loss, a suspicious fundus presentation, maybe some subretinal fluid on OCT, and yet your fluorescein angiogram came back relatively unremarkable? You know something is wrong. Your clinical instincts are firing. But the FA just isn't giving you the answer. That scenario is exactly where ICG angiography earns its place in the diagnostic toolkit.

So let's lay the groundwork first. Fluorescein angiography has been the gold standard for retinal vascular imaging for decades, and it remains incredibly valuable. But fluorescein has a fundamental limitation. The dye molecules are relatively small, and they leak readily from the choriocapillaris. On top of that, the retinal pigment epithelium, the RPE, acts as a barrier that partially blocks the fluorescence signal from the choroid. So when pathology is primarily choroidal, fluorescein can miss it entirely, or at best give you a blurry, nonspecific picture.

ICG dye is different in a very important way. Indocyanine green binds tightly to plasma proteins, which means it stays within the choroidal vasculature much longer. It also fluoresces in the near-infrared spectrum, around 835 nanometers, and near-infrared light penetrates the RPE, subretinal fluid, lipid exudates, and even thin layers of hemorrhage far more effectively than the visible light used in fluorescein imaging. The result is that ICG gives you a direct, high-resolution window into the choroidal circulation that fluorescein simply cannot provide. That's not a minor technical difference. That's a clinically transformative difference.

Now let's get into the first major clinical scenario where ICG changes the game. Occult choroidal neovascularization.

In neovascular age-related macular degeneration, we classify CNV into classic and occult subtypes based on fluorescein angiography. Classic CNV shows up as a well-defined area of early hyperfluorescence with progressive leakage. It's relatively easy to identify on FA. But occult CNV is a different story. On fluorescein, occult CNV presents as either a fibrovascular pigment epithelial detachment, or as late-phase leakage of undetermined source. The boundaries are poorly defined. The source of the leakage is unclear. And that ambiguity makes treatment planning difficult.

On ICG angiography, occult CNV often reveals itself as a focal hot spot, a discrete area of hyperfluorescence in the mid to late phases of the study. These hot spots correspond to the actual neovascular complex beneath the RPE, and they can guide laser treatment, photodynamic therapy planning, or anti-VEGF injection targeting with much greater precision. Studies have shown that ICG identifies a definable neovascular lesion in a significant proportion of cases that appear purely occult on fluorescein. For your patients with neovascular AMD who aren't responding to anti-VEGF therapy as expected, or where the lesion boundaries are unclear, ICG can be the imaging modality that finally gives the treating retinal specialist the roadmap they need.

From a chairside perspective, here's what should trigger your thinking. A patient over sixty with decreased central vision, metamorphopsia on Amsler grid testing, and on fundus examination you see subretinal fluid, a pigment epithelial detachment, or subtle subretinal hemorrhage. Your OCT shows irregular RPE elevation, maybe a double-layer sign, or hyperreflective material beneath the RPE. Your FA is inconclusive or shows only late nonspecific leakage. That's your ICG moment. That's when your referral note to the retinal specialist should specifically request ICG angiography, not just a standard FA.

Now let's move to the second scenario, and this one is critically underdiagnosed in general optometric practice. Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, or PCV.

PCV is a distinct choroidal vascular disorder characterized by an inner choroidal vascular network that terminates in polypoidal, aneurysmal dilations. It was historically considered a variant of AMD, but it's now recognized as a separate entity with its own pathophysiology, its own natural history, and importantly, its own treatment implications. PCV is particularly prevalent in Asian and African American populations, though it occurs across all ethnicities. It can present in patients who are younger than your typical AMD demographic, sometimes in their fifties or even late forties.

Clinically, PCV can look deceptively like wet AMD. Patients present with decreased vision, metamorphopsia, and you may see orange-red subretinal nodules on fundus examination, which correspond to the polypoidal lesions. You'll often see large serous or hemorrhagic pigment epithelial detachments, sometimes with a notched or irregular contour. Subretinal hemorrhage can be extensive. On OCT, you may see a thumb-like protrusion at the base of a PED, which is a classic sign of a polyp, along with double-layer sign and hyporeflective spaces within the PED.

Here's the critical point. Fluorescein angiography is often nonspecific in PCV. It may show a pattern consistent with occult CNV, or it may show a branching vascular network with late staining, but the polypoidal lesions themselves are frequently not well visualized. ICG angiography is the definitive diagnostic tool for PCV. On ICG, the branching vascular network and the polypoidal lesions light up brilliantly in the early to mid phases, giving a characteristic grape-like cluster appearance. This is pathognomonic. You cannot make a confident diagnosis of PCV without ICG.

Why does this matter clinically? Because PCV responds differently to treatment than typical neovascular AMD. Anti-VEGF monotherapy has lower efficacy in PCV compared to AMD. The current evidence, including data from the EVEREST II trial, supports combination therapy with anti-VEGF agents plus photodynamic therapy for PCV, particularly for lesions with active polyps. If your patient is being treated for presumed wet AMD and not responding well, PCV should be on your differential, and ICG should be requested.

As the primary eye care provider, your role is to recognize the clinical pattern, document your findings thoroughly, and make a timely referral with a specific request for ICG angiography. Don't just write refer for wet AMD evaluation. Write refer for evaluation of possible polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy, please consider ICG angiography. That specificity matters. It guides the specialist and it accelerates the diagnostic process for your patient.

Let's move to our third major category. Choroidal tumors.

The choroid is the most vascularized tissue in the body, and it's a site where both primary and metastatic tumors can develop. The differential diagnosis for a choroidal mass includes choroidal melanoma, choroidal nevus, choroidal hemangioma, choroidal metastasis, and choroidal osteoma, among others. Getting this differential right is not academic. It is life-altering for your patient.

Choroidal melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults. It can present as a pigmented or amelanotic subretinal mass, often with overlying orange lipofuscin pigment, subretinal fluid, and visual field defects corresponding to the lesion location. The classic mnemonic for risk factors of malignant transformation in a choroidal nevus is To Find Small Ocular Melanoma, which stands for Thickness greater than two millimeters, subretinal Fluid, Symptoms, Orange pigment, Margin within three millimeters of the disc, ultrasonographic Hollowness, and absence of Halo. These are your clinical red flags.

Now, where does ICG fit in with choroidal tumors? Choroidal hemangiomas are a particularly important example. Circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors that can cause exudative retinal detachment and significant vision loss if untreated. On fluorescein angiography, they show early hyperfluorescence, but the pattern can overlap with amelanotic melanoma, making differentiation challenging. On ICG angiography, circumscribed choroidal hemangiomas show a very characteristic early, intense hyperfluorescence in the prearterial phase, followed by washout in the late phase. This pattern is highly specific and can help distinguish hemangioma from melanoma without requiring more invasive testing.

For choroidal melanomas, ICG can help delineate tumor vascularity and extent, which is valuable for treatment planning. For metastatic lesions, which are often multiple and bilateral, ICG can help characterize the vascular pattern and extent of choroidal involvement.

Your role as the optometrist in these cases is early detection and urgent referral. Any suspicious choroidal lesion warrants prompt referral to an ocular oncologist or a retinal specialist with oncology experience. Document the lesion size, location, associated features, and your OCT findings. B-scan ultrasonography is also a critical adjunct, particularly for assessing lesion thickness and internal reflectivity. But ICG, in the hands of the specialist, will often be part of the comprehensive workup.

Let's bring this all together with some practical takeaways you can apply starting tomorrow.

First, when you have a patient with unexplained vision loss, subretinal fluid, or a PED that doesn't fit neatly into your FA findings, think ICG. Don't just accept an inconclusive fluorescein study as the end of the diagnostic road.

Second, in patients with suspected neovascular AMD who are not responding to anti-VEGF therapy, put PCV on your differential and specifically request ICG in your referral.

Third, for any suspicious choroidal mass, especially when you're trying to differentiate hemangioma from melanoma, know that ICG is part of the specialist's toolkit and mention it in your referral communication.

Fourth, document everything meticulously. Your OCT findings, your fundus photography, your clinical observations. The more information you send with your referral, the faster the specialist can move to the right diagnostic test.

And fifth, stay current. The evidence base for ICG angiography continues to grow, particularly with the advent of swept-source OCT angiography, which is beginning to provide some of the choroidal detail that ICG offers in a non-invasive format. But ICG remains the gold standard for choroidal vascular imaging, and understanding its role makes you a better clinician and a better advocate for your patients.

The choroid is not a passive bystander in posterior segment disease. It is an active, dynamic tissue where some of the most vision-threatening pathology originates. Fluorescein shows you the retina. ICG shows you what's underneath. And sometimes, what's underneath is exactly what your patient needs you to find.

Thank you so much for spending this time with me today. I hope this episode gives you a sharper clinical lens, pun absolutely intended, for approaching choroidal pathology in your practice. If you found this valuable, share it with a colleague, a resident, or anyone in your clinical circle who would benefit.

Visit Focus Cast at Focuslinks dot in for more episodes, clinical resources, and continuing education content built specifically for eye care professionals like you. Until next time, keep looking deeper, keep asking better questions, and keep protecting the vision of the patients who trust you with their eyes.

Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want sharp, clinically relevant content delivered straight to their ears. I'm glad you're here, and today we are diving deep into one of the most consequential conditions you will encounter in your exam chair, week after week, year after year. We're talking about diabetic retinopathy, and specifically, how to stage it with precision, from the earliest whisper of mild non-proliferative disease all the way through to the vision-threatening chaos of proliferative diabetic retinopathy. If you've ever stood at the slit lamp looking at a fundus and asked yourself, is this mild, is this moderate, do I refer today or do I watch, then this episode is exactly for you.

Let's set the stage with a number that should stop you in your tracks. Diabetic retinopathy remains the leading cause of new blindness in working-age adults in developed countries. And here's the clinical reality, most of those patients saw an eye care provider before they lost vision. Which means the staging decisions we make, the referral thresholds we apply, and the documentation we produce are not administrative exercises. They are the difference between preserved vision and permanent visual impairment. So let's get into the science and the clinical craft of staging this disease properly.

We're going to work through four main areas today. First, the ETDRS-derived severity scale and why it matters clinically. Second, what each stage actually looks like when you're at the slit lamp or reviewing your fundus images. Third, how to think through differential diagnosis at each stage. And fourth, the chairside decision-making framework that should guide your management and referral patterns. Let's go.

The Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study, the ETDRS, is the foundational clinical trial that gave us the grading system we still use today. Published in the late 1980s and early 1990s, this landmark study enrolled over 3700 patients and gave us not just treatment data but a rigorous photographic grading scale that stratified retinopathy severity into reproducible, prognostically meaningful categories. The International Clinical Diabetic Retinopathy Disease Severity Scale, which was derived from ETDRS data and simplified for clinical use in 2003, is what most of us apply in practice. It gives us five levels. No apparent retinopathy. Mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy, or mild NPDR. Moderate NPDR. Severe NPDR. And proliferative diabetic retinopathy, PDR. Each level carries a specific set of funduscopic findings and, critically, a specific risk of progression. Understanding that risk is what drives your clinical decisions.

Let's walk through each stage now, and I want you to picture yourself at the slit lamp with a 90-diopter lens, or reviewing a widefield fundus image, because that's where this knowledge lives.

Mild NPDR is defined by the presence of at least one microaneurysm and nothing more. That's it. One microaneurysm. These appear as tiny, discrete, round red dots, typically in the posterior pole, often near the macula. They are the earliest clinically visible sign of retinal vascular compromise. Histologically, they represent focal outpouchings of the capillary wall due to pericyte loss, which is one of the earliest cellular events in diabetic retinopathy. At the slit lamp with a 90D lens, they can be subtle. They're smaller than a dot hemorrhage, they have a more defined border, and they don't have the feathered edges you'd see with a flame hemorrhage. Fluorescein angiography, if you have access to it, will show these as hyperfluorescent dots with late leakage. The annual risk of progression from mild NPDR to PDR is relatively low, around 5 percent over five years, but that doesn't mean you ignore it. It means you establish a baseline, counsel the patient on systemic control, and bring them back in 12 months.

Moderate NPDR is where things start to get more interesting and more concerning. Here you're seeing more than just microaneurysms. You're seeing hard exudates, which are those crisp, waxy, yellow-white deposits of lipid and protein that leak from damaged capillaries. You're seeing dot and blot hemorrhages, which are intraretinal hemorrhages in the deeper nuclear layers. You may be seeing cotton wool spots, which are nerve fiber layer infarcts appearing as fluffy white superficial lesions. And you may be seeing mild venous beading. The key distinction between moderate and severe NPDR is the 4-2-1 rule, which we'll get to in a moment. In moderate NPDR, you have these findings but you haven't crossed the threshold of the 4-2-1 rule. The five-year risk of progression to PDR from moderate NPDR is approximately 12 to 27 percent depending on the study population. Your follow-up interval here tightens to every 6 months, and if there's any diabetic macular edema present, your management changes significantly.

Now let's talk about severe NPDR, because this is the stage where your clinical antenna needs to be fully extended. Severe NPDR is defined by the 4-2-1 rule, and you need to have this memorized. The patient has severe NPDR if they have any one of the following three findings. Intraretinal hemorrhages and microaneurysms in all four quadrants. Venous beading in two or more quadrants. Or intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, what we call IRMA, in at least one quadrant. IRMA are dilated, tortuous intraretinal vessels that represent shunt vessels bypassing areas of capillary non-perfusion. They look like irregular, looping vascular channels within the retina, and they are a critical sign because they indicate significant ischemia. The one-year risk of progression from severe NPDR to PDR is approximately 15 percent, and the one-year risk of developing high-risk PDR is around 45 percent. These patients need to be seen every 3 to 4 months, and a retinal specialist consultation is strongly warranted. You are not watching and waiting here. You are actively co-managing.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy represents the transition from a disease of vascular leakage and occlusion to a disease of pathological neovascularization. The ischemic retina upregulates vascular endothelial growth factor, VEGF, and that VEGF drives the growth of new, fragile, abnormal vessels on the surface of the retina and into the vitreous. These new vessels, called neovascularization, can arise from the disc, which we call NVD, or elsewhere in the retina, which we call NVE. NVD is particularly ominous. At the slit lamp with your 90D lens, neovascularization appears as fine, lacy, irregular vascular fronds on the inner retinal surface or extending into the vitreous. They may be subtle early on, and this is where your stereoscopic viewing technique matters. You need to be looking in three dimensions to appreciate vessels that are elevated off the retinal plane. High-risk PDR is defined by the presence of NVD greater than one-third disc area, any NVD with vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage, or NVE greater than one-half disc area with vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage. These patients need same-day or next-day retinal referral. This is not a situation where you schedule a routine referral and move on. You are picking up the phone.

Let's spend a moment on differential diagnosis, because not every red dot is a microaneurysm and not every white lesion is a cotton wool spot. When you're looking at a fundus with dot hemorrhages and microaneurysms, you need to consider hypertensive retinopathy, which can produce a very similar picture. The key differentiator is the arteriovenous changes you'll see in hypertension, including AV nicking, arterial attenuation, and the distribution of hemorrhages, which in hypertension tend to be more flame-shaped and in the nerve fiber layer. Retinal vein occlusion can also produce quadrant-based hemorrhages that might superficially resemble severe NPDR, but the distribution follows a vascular territory rather than being diffuse. Radiation retinopathy, sickle cell retinopathy, and even HIV retinopathy can produce cotton wool spots and microaneurysms. Your history is your first diagnostic tool. A patient with a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes and an HbA1c of 9.5 presenting with bilateral dot hemorrhages is almost certainly diabetic retinopathy. But always correlate with the clinical picture.

Now let's talk about chairside decision-making, because this is where the rubber meets the road. Your staging determines your follow-up interval, your referral urgency, and your documentation. For mild NPDR with no diabetic macular edema, annual follow-up is appropriate. For moderate NPDR, every 6 months. For severe NPDR, every 3 to 4 months with retinal co-management. For PDR, immediate referral. But here's a nuance that often gets overlooked. Diabetic macular edema, or DME, can occur at any stage of retinopathy and is actually the most common cause of vision loss in diabetic patients. You need to be evaluating the macula at every diabetic eye exam. OCT is your best friend here. Spectral-domain OCT will show you subretinal fluid, intraretinal cysts, and loss of the foveal contour with a sensitivity that clinical examination alone cannot match. If you see center-involving DME on OCT, that patient needs anti-VEGF therapy, and that means a retinal specialist is involved regardless of the NPDR stage.

Your documentation also matters enormously. Use the International Clinical Severity Scale terminology in your notes. Write mild NPDR, moderate NPDR, severe NPDR, or PDR. Document the specific findings you observed. Document whether DME is present or absent. Document your referral decision and the urgency. This protects your patient, it protects you, and it creates a longitudinal record that is clinically invaluable.

One final thought before we close. Diabetic retinopathy is a disease where optometrists are often the first and sometimes the only eye care provider a patient sees regularly. That is a profound responsibility and a profound opportunity. When you stage this disease accurately, when you counsel patients on the relationship between glycemic control and retinal outcomes, when you make the right referral at the right time, you are practicing at the absolute top of your scope. The ETDRS gave us the science. Your clinical skills and your judgment are what translate that science into preserved vision for your patients.

Thank you so much for spending this time with me today. I hope this episode gives you a sharper, more confident framework the next time you're at the slit lamp staging diabetic retinopathy. Keep asking the hard questions, keep refining your clinical skills, and keep showing up for your patients with the expertise they deserve. For more clinically focused content built specifically for eye care professionals, visit Focus Cast at Focuslinks dot in. Until next time, keep your lenses clean and your clinical thinking even cleaner.

Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want sharp, clinically relevant content delivered straight to their ears. I'm glad you're here today, because we're diving into a topic that sits right at the intersection of chronic disease management and sight-saving intervention. We're talking about diabetic macular edema, specifically the criteria for clinically significant macular edema, and the OCT features that should be pushing you toward anti-VEGF thresholds. If you've ever sat across from a diabetic patient, squinted at their fundus, and asked yourself, is this bad enough to refer today, then this episode is exactly for you.

Let's set the stage. Diabetes is one of the most common systemic conditions walking through your exam lane every single day. And while we spend a lot of time thinking about diabetic retinopathy staging, it's actually diabetic macular edema, or DME, that is the leading cause of vision loss in working-age adults with diabetes. Not proliferative disease. Not neovascularization of the disc. Macular edema. That fluid accumulating in the very center of the retina, threatening the photoreceptors your patient depends on to read, drive, and recognize faces. So understanding when edema crosses the line from something you monitor to something you act on, that's the clinical skill we're sharpening today.

Let's start with the foundation. The term clinically significant macular edema, or CSME, comes from the Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study, the ETDRS, which was published back in the 1980s. And even though our imaging technology has evolved dramatically since then, those criteria remain clinically relevant and are still referenced in practice today. CSME is defined by three specific findings on biomicroscopic examination. First, retinal thickening at or within five hundred microns of the center of the macula. Second, hard exudates at or within five hundred microns of the center, with associated thickening of the adjacent retina. And third, a zone of retinal thickening one disc area or larger in size, any part of which is within one disc diameter of the center of the macula. If any one of those three criteria is met, you have CSME. Full stop.

Now here's where it gets practically important. CSME is a clinical diagnosis. It was originally defined using slit lamp biomicroscopy with a contact or non-contact fundus lens, typically a 78 or 90 diopter lens, or a Goldmann three-mirror contact lens. You're looking for that subtle elevation of the retinal surface, the loss of the normal foveal reflex, and the presence of hard exudates clustering near the center. Hard exudates, by the way, are those bright yellow lipid deposits that form at the outer boundary of edematous retina. They're a sign that fluid has been there long enough to leave a residue. When you see a ring or circinate pattern of hard exudates pointing toward the fovea, your antenna should go up immediately.

But let's be honest. Biomicroscopy alone has its limits. Detecting subtle central thickening with a slit lamp takes experience, and even experienced clinicians can miss early or moderate edema without objective imaging. That's where optical coherence tomography, OCT, has completely transformed our management of DME. And this brings us to our second major segment, the OCT features that define treatment thresholds.

Spectral domain OCT is now the gold standard for evaluating DME. It gives you quantitative retinal thickness measurements, structural detail of the retinal layers, and the ability to track change over time with precision that no fundus lens can match. When you're looking at an OCT of a patient with DME, there are several key features you need to identify and document. The first is central subfield thickness, or CST. This is the average retinal thickness within the central one millimeter circle on your macular thickness map. Normal CST is generally around two hundred fifty to three hundred microns, though this varies slightly by instrument and by sex, with men typically having slightly thicker retinas than women. When CST exceeds three hundred and twenty to three hundred and fifty microns, depending on your reference values, that's a flag. When it exceeds four hundred microns, you're looking at significant edema that almost certainly warrants intervention.

But thickness alone doesn't tell the whole story. You also need to look at the morphological features on the B-scan. Intraretinal cystoid spaces, those dark hyporeflective pockets within the retinal layers, particularly in the outer nuclear layer and Henle's fiber layer, are a hallmark of DME. Subretinal fluid, which appears as a hyporeflective space between the photoreceptor layer and the retinal pigment epithelium, can also be present and is associated with more severe or chronic edema. Disorganization of the retinal inner layers, sometimes abbreviated as DRIL, is a particularly important finding because it correlates strongly with reduced visual acuity and a poorer prognosis for visual recovery even after treatment. And then there's the integrity of the ellipsoid zone, that bright hyperreflective band corresponding to the inner segment and outer segment junction of the photoreceptors. Disruption of the ellipsoid zone in the foveal region is a sign of photoreceptor stress or damage, and it tells you that the edema has been present long enough to start affecting the cells you most want to protect.

So when you're sitting at your OCT workstation reviewing a diabetic patient's scan, you're not just looking at a number. You're looking at the architecture of the macula and asking, how much damage has already occurred, and how urgently does this patient need treatment.

Now let's talk about the anti-VEGF threshold, because this is where optometrists in co-management roles need to be especially clear. Vascular endothelial growth factor, VEGF, is the primary driver of vascular permeability in DME. Anti-VEGF agents, including ranibizumab, bevacizumab, and aflibercept, have become the first-line treatment for center-involving DME, which is edema that affects the central subfield of the macula. The landmark clinical trials, including RIDE, RISE, PROTOCOL T, and DRCR Retina Network studies, have consistently shown that anti-VEGF therapy leads to significant gains in visual acuity and reduction in retinal thickness in patients with center-involving DME.

The key clinical decision point is this. If your patient has center-involving DME with a CST above the threshold for their instrument, and particularly if their best corrected visual acuity is worse than twenty over twenty-five, that patient needs to be in the hands of a retinal specialist for anti-VEGF consideration. This is not a watch and wait situation. Every month of untreated center-involving DME is a month of ongoing photoreceptor stress. The DRCR Protocol V study did show that some patients with good vision and center-involving DME can be observed initially, but that requires close monitoring, typically every one to three months with OCT, and a low threshold to escalate to treatment if vision drops or edema worsens.

For non-center-involving DME, where the thickening spares the central subfield, the approach can be more conservative. Focal or grid laser photocoagulation may still have a role here, particularly for edema associated with focal leaking microaneurysms. But even in these cases, close follow-up and excellent documentation are essential.

Let's move into our third segment, differential diagnosis and chairside decision-making. Not every macular thickening in a diabetic patient is DME. You need to keep your differential sharp. Epiretinal membrane, or ERM, can cause macular thickening and distortion that mimics edema on OCT. Look for the hyperreflective line on the inner retinal surface and the characteristic wrinkling or traction of the inner retinal layers. Vitreomacular traction can also cause macular thickening and may coexist with DME, complicating the clinical picture. Age-related macular degeneration with subretinal fluid can look similar, though the clinical context and the presence of drusen or RPE changes will help you differentiate. And don't forget that hypertensive retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, and uveitic macular edema can all produce cystoid macular edema patterns on OCT that require different management pathways.

At the chair, your decision-making framework should be systematic. Start with a thorough history. How long has the patient had diabetes? What's their HbA1c? Are they on insulin? Have they had any prior laser or injection treatment? Then move to your examination. Check best corrected visual acuity carefully, because a drop in acuity is often the first symptom a patient notices. Perform dilated fundus examination with a 78 or 90 diopter lens, looking specifically for the CSME criteria we discussed. Then get your OCT. Document the CST, the morphological features, and compare to any prior imaging. If you see center-involving edema with reduced acuity, your referral should go out the same day or within the week. If you see non-center-involving edema with good acuity, schedule a follow-up in four to six weeks and communicate clearly with the patient about warning signs, specifically any sudden decrease in vision, new distortion, or metamorphopsia.

And speaking of patient communication, this is a moment to reinforce the systemic connection. Tight glycemic control, blood pressure management, and lipid control all influence the course of DME. You're not prescribing those medications, but you are the clinician who sees this patient regularly and who can reinforce the importance of working with their primary care physician or endocrinologist. Your voice carries weight in that conversation.

As we wrap up today, let's bring it all together. Diabetic macular edema is a sight-threatening condition that demands precise clinical recognition and timely action. The ETDRS CSME criteria give you a biomicroscopic framework. OCT gives you the objective data, the central subfield thickness, the cystoid spaces, the ellipsoid zone integrity, and the DRIL findings that guide your treatment threshold decisions. Center-involving DME with reduced acuity is your anti-VEGF referral trigger. Non-center-involving DME requires close monitoring and a low threshold to escalate. And your differential diagnosis skills keep you from missing the other conditions that can masquerade as DME.

Every diabetic patient in your chair is trusting you to catch this before it steals their central vision. That's a responsibility worth taking seriously, and it's one that optometrists are uniquely positioned to fulfill through consistent, high-quality retinal evaluation.

Thank you so much for spending these ten minutes with me today. I hope this episode gives you something concrete to take back into your exam lane tomorrow. For more clinical content built specifically for optometrists and eye care professionals, visit Focus Cast at Focuslinks dot in. Until next time, keep your lenses clean and your clinical thinking sharper.

episodes.content:
Welcome to Focus Cast by Focuslinks dot in, the podcast built for eye care professionals who want sharp, clinically relevant content delivered straight to their ears. I'm glad you're here, and today we are diving deep into a topic that sits right at the intersection of what optometrists need to understand about retinal disease management, and that topic is Panretinal Photocoagulation, or PRP.

Now, you might be thinking, PRP is something the retinal specialist does, not me. And you are right that the laser itself is performed by a retinal surgeon or an ophthalmologist. But here is the thing. Your patient is going to walk into your chair before the laser, after the laser, and sometimes years after the laser, and they are going to have questions, symptoms, and findings that you need to interpret accurately. So today, we are going to make sure you are fully equipped to do exactly that.

Let us start with the foundation. What is Panretinal Photocoagulation, and why does it exist?

PRP is a laser treatment applied to the peripheral retina, typically in a scatter pattern, with the goal of destroying ischemic retinal tissue. The logic is elegant in a brutal sort of way. When the peripheral retina becomes ischemic, it releases vascular endothelial growth factor, or VEGF. That VEGF drives neovascularization, which is the growth of fragile, abnormal new blood vessels. Those new vessels can bleed into the vitreous, cause tractional retinal detachment, or grow onto the iris and angle, leading to neovascular glaucoma. PRP destroys the ischemic tissue, reduces the VEGF load, and causes regression of those neovascular vessels. It is not a cure. It is a controlled sacrifice of peripheral retinal tissue to save the central vision and the eye itself.

The primary indications you need to have memorized are proliferative diabetic retinopathy, which is the most common indication by far, proliferative sickle cell retinopathy, central retinal vein occlusion with neovascularization, and branch retinal vein occlusion with neovascularization. You may also see PRP used in cases of retinal arterial macroaneurysm with associated ischemia, or in certain presentations of Coats disease. But in your day-to-day practice, diabetic retinopathy is going to be the big one.

The Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study, the ETDRS, gave us the landmark evidence base for PRP. High-risk proliferative diabetic retinopathy, defined by neovascularization of the disc greater than one-quarter to one-third disc area, any neovascularization with vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage, or neovascularization elsewhere greater than one-half disc area with hemorrhage, these are the thresholds that trigger the conversation about PRP. When you see these findings on dilated fundus exam or on widefield fundus imaging, your job is to recognize them and refer urgently.

Now let us talk about what you are actually going to see when you examine a post-PRP patient. This is where your clinical skills really matter.

When you dilate a patient who has had PRP, the fundus appearance is distinctive. You will see multiple, discrete, round to oval laser scars scattered throughout the mid-peripheral and far peripheral retina. In the early post-laser period, these scars appear as pale, whitish lesions with surrounding pigmentation. Over time, they evolve. The scars become more pigmented, often developing a hyperpigmented border with a central area of chorioretinal atrophy. The retinal pigment epithelium, the RPE, is disrupted, and you can see through to the underlying choroid in some areas. On fundus photography, these scars have a classic moth-eaten or punched-out appearance scattered across the peripheral fundus.

The number of laser spots varies. A full PRP treatment typically involves somewhere between 1200 and 1600 spots, though some patients receive more, especially if the neovascularization was extensive or if they required retreatment. When you are doing your dilated exam, count the quadrants involved. PRP is usually applied in all four quadrants, sparing the macula and the area within two disc diameters of the optic nerve. If you see laser scars encroaching on the posterior pole, that is worth noting and discussing with the retinal specialist.

On OCT, post-PRP scars show disruption of the outer retinal layers, including the ellipsoid zone and the RPE band, in the areas corresponding to the laser burns. The inner retinal layers are generally preserved because the laser energy is targeted at the outer retina and RPE. If you are doing widefield OCT or OCT with peripheral scanning, you can actually visualize these scars in cross-section, which is a great teaching moment for your patients.

Now here is the segment that I think is most practically valuable for your chairside work. What are your patients going to tell you after PRP, and how do you interpret those complaints?

The most common complaint after PRP is reduced peripheral vision. This is expected and it is permanent. PRP destroys peripheral retinal tissue, and that tissue does not regenerate. Patients will often describe difficulty driving at night, trouble seeing in their peripheral field, or a sense that their side vision has narrowed. When you do visual field testing on a post-PRP patient, you will typically find peripheral constriction, often with relative scotomas corresponding to the laser scar locations. This is not a complication. It is the expected outcome of the treatment. Your job is to counsel the patient appropriately and document the baseline field so you can monitor for any progression.

The second major complaint is reduced night vision, or nocturia, which patients sometimes describe as difficulty adjusting when going from a bright environment to a dark one. The peripheral retina is rich in rod photoreceptors, and PRP destroys a significant number of them. This is again expected and permanent. Counsel your patients to use extra caution when driving at night, and consider whether any of your low vision resources might be helpful for patients who are significantly affected.

The third complaint you will hear is glare and photophobia, particularly in the early post-laser period. The laser burns cause an inflammatory response, and patients may experience significant light sensitivity for days to weeks after treatment. This typically resolves as the scars mature. If a patient presents with severe photophobia weeks or months after PRP, you want to rule out other causes, including uveitis, elevated IOP, or corneal issues.

Speaking of IOP, this is something you must check in every post-PRP patient. PRP can cause a transient elevation in intraocular pressure in the immediate post-laser period, related to inflammation and angle changes. More importantly, if the underlying disease process has caused neovascularization of the iris, called rubeosis iridis, or neovascularization of the angle, the patient is at risk for neovascular glaucoma. On your slit lamp exam, look carefully at the iris surface and the pupillary margin for fine, lacy new vessels. On gonioscopy, which you should be performing in these patients, look for neovascularization of the angle. Neovascular glaucoma is a devastating complication, and early detection is critical.

Let us also talk about what you might see on refraction and anterior segment exam. Post-PRP patients can develop a transient myopic shift in the early post-laser period. This is thought to be related to ciliary body edema and forward rotation of the lens-iris diaphragm. If a patient comes in shortly after PRP with a new myopic shift, do not just update the glasses. Recognize this as a physiologic response to the laser treatment and counsel the patient that the refraction may stabilize over the following weeks. Repeat the refraction once the acute inflammatory phase has resolved.

On slit lamp exam, you may also see anterior chamber flare and cells in the early post-laser period, consistent with the inflammatory response. Posterior synechiae can form if the inflammation is significant. Check the lens for any new posterior subcapsular changes, as diabetic patients are already at elevated risk for cataract, and the inflammatory response from PRP can accelerate lens changes.

Now let us talk about your role in the ongoing management of these patients, because this is where optometry adds tremendous value.

Your post-PRP patient needs regular monitoring. At minimum, you should be performing dilated fundus exams every three to six months, depending on the stability of their disease. You are looking for regression of neovascularization, which is the goal of PRP, but you are also watching for recurrence. Neovascularization can recur if the ischemic drive is not fully controlled, and some patients require additional laser sessions or adjunctive anti-VEGF injections. If you see new neovascularization, preretinal hemorrhage, or vitreous hemorrhage on your exam, that patient needs to go back to the retinal specialist promptly.

OCT of the macula is essential in these patients. Diabetic macular edema can coexist with proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and PRP itself can sometimes worsen macular edema by increasing VEGF release acutely. If your patient has decreased visual acuity after PRP, do not assume it is just from the laser. Get an OCT of the macula and look for edema. This is a treatable condition, and early detection leads to better outcomes.

Widefield fundus photography is your best friend for longitudinal monitoring. Photograph the peripheral retina at each visit and compare to prior images. This allows you to objectively document regression of neovascularization, stability of laser scars, and any new findings. It also gives you a powerful communication tool when you are coordinating care with the retinal specialist.

And finally, never forget the systemic picture. Your diabetic patient's retinal disease is a window into their overall vascular health. If you are seeing progression of retinopathy despite PRP, that is a signal to communicate with their primary care physician or endocrinologist about glycemic control, blood pressure management, and lipid levels. You are not just an eye doctor. You are part of a care team, and your observations matter.

So let us bring this all together. PRP is a powerful, vision-saving treatment for proliferative retinal disease. As an optometrist, you need to recognize the indications, identify the post-laser fundus appearance, interpret your patient's visual complaints accurately, monitor for complications including neovascular glaucoma and macular edema, and coordinate care effectively with your retinal colleagues. The patient who has had PRP is not a finished case. They are an ongoing management challenge, and your clinical expertise is essential to their long-term outcomes.

Thank you so much for spending this time with me today. I hope this episode gives you the clinical confidence to manage your post-PRP patients with precision and purpose. For more evidence-based content built specifically for eye care professionals, visit Focus Cast at Focuslinks dot in. Until next time, keep your optics sharp and your clinical thinking sharper.
